added_claim_errors: "Leaving the full $1,900 untouched risks forfeiting roughly $1,220–$1,240": the $1,240 end of the range uses the 2025 $660 cap, which does not apply to a 2026 plan year. The sentence also understates the no-feature case, where all $1,900 is at risk (minor).
"at most $660 of 2025 funds can move into 2026": wrong plan year. The plan year ending Dec 31 is 2026, so the cap is $680 carried into 2027.

"Grace period — you can incur expenses through March 15, 2026": wrong year (the latest possible date is March 15, 2027). It is also stated as a fixed date when March 15 is only the maximum and plans may set a shorter period.

"So at most $660 of your $1,900 survives... The March dental work does not get to spend the other $1,240": wrong under a grace period, where all $1,900 can pay for work done by the grace end. It also contradicts B's own later grace-period caveat.
$1,240 forfeited: wrong for 2026. The correct figure is $1,900 - $680 = $1,220.

reasons: Both answers correct the rollover premise at the start. Both give the no-prepayment rule and tell the person to call HR, and both leave out the 2027 open-enrollment election. A gets the 2026 carryover cap right ($680). It frames the grace period as up to 2½ months, typically through March 15, with a reminder to confirm the date, and lays out all three branches correctly; its only slip is a $1,220–$1,240 range that mixes in the 2025 cap. B is a year off throughout: it uses the $660 cap for 2025 funds and a March 15, 2026 grace end. It also says flatly that at most $660 survives and the March work cannot use the other $1,240. That is wrong if the plan has a grace period, and it could steer the person away from a valid option. B's list of eligible items is better, but its core figures and dates are less reliable.
